newsitem.title: UK: Britain's W.H.Smith catches bid fever.
newsitem.headline: Britain's W.H.Smith catches bid fever.

text.p: Britain's best known book-shop chain W.H. Smith Group Plc was back in the spotlight this week as a potential bid target with suggestions that supermarket giant Tesco Plc could be on the prowl.
The struggling retailer's shares bounded ahead on the speculation, gaining 10 pence on Monday to 466.5.
But the shares edged down a penny at the opening on Tuesday, and retail analysts were not convinced that Smith's business offered tempting enough goodies to attract a predator.

Tesco, keen on diversification, is known to be looking to expand its smaller, town-centre Metro stores. But analysts said buying Smiths, valued at around two billion pounds ($3.4 billion), would be an expensive way of doing it.
"I think to take this method to get a few more shops would be a bit excessive," said one retail analyst who asked not to be identified.

Talk of a major bid hitting Britain's retail sector has gathered momentum over the past month, with names such as Sears Plc, House of Fraser Plc and Storehouse Plc all tipped as potential candidates. In December there were reports that Boots Co Plc had looked at Smiths.

This latest flurry followed a badly-handled share buy order last week which traders said squeezed Smith's shares higher. An article in The Sunday Telegraph newspaper at the weekend, highlighting Tesco as a potential bidder added to the bid fever.
A spokeswoman said Tesco did not comment on such market speculation and a Smith spokesman also had no comment on the bid rumours.

W.H. Smith, one of the best-known names on Britain's shopping streets, has looked vulnerable to a takeover since it started to lose ground in its once-dominant market position in books, stationery and newspapers to supermarket chains such as Tesco and ASDA Group Plc. Last August the firm reported the first loss in its 204-year history.

It brought in a new chief executive Bill Cockburn last year, who has shaken up management, sold off the Smith's share of the home improvement chain Do It All, the Niceday office supplies business and Paperchase to try and get back into profit.
Analysts say there are still problems with the main chain, even though it may get some relief from a strong Christmas sales.
"There are still problems in the main chain," said Clive Vaughan at retail consultants Verdict Research. "W.H. Smith doesn't sell anything that you can't get somewhere else."

Analysts recognise it has a superb brand name, and a huge retail estate, with stores in almost every major town centre. It also has attractive specialist businesses in Waterstones, the upmarket bookseller, and Virgin/Our Price music stores.
But the group's problems probably outweigh its attractions for any would-be bidder.
Some analysts said the stock looked unattractive at these levels. "It's driven by bid speculation, but it doesn't seem justified," said one, who asked not to be identified.
Broker BZW predicts the group will make pre-tax profits in the year to May 1997 of 115 million sterling, putting Smith on a multiple of 18 times, a 24 percent premium to the market. ($1=.5921 Pound)
